sentences.text: Mature Kambara crocodilians generally reached lengths between 3 and 4 meters, making them medium-sized compared to later mekosuchines like Baru and Paludirex.

The animal possessed a roughly triangular skull that was narrow at the snout tip and widened toward the back, featuring an upper jaw overbite where the teeth overlapped the lower jaw, similar to modern alligators.
The humerus of Kambara was much straighter than in modern crocodiles, with both articulating surfaces level to each other.
The largest known Kambara, represented by a large mandible, may have reached lengths of up to 3.5 meters.

A fossilized plastron of Kambara taraina bears linear circular pits matching the bite marks of a crocodile, suggesting the turtle was bitten repeatedly in a behavior similar to the "juggling" seen in modern crocodiles.

The Murgon fossil site preserves bones of hatchling-sized Kambara individuals and fragmentary egg shells, while one adult fossil shows a fibula deformed to be twice as wide as normal in some areas, possibly due to a tumor.
Kambara fossils are among the oldest Tertiary fossils found in Australia, dating to about 55 million years ago, and the genus is the oldest known Mekosuchinae.
Kambara remains were first formally described by Ralph Molnar in 1982, initially thought to belong to a Miocene crocodylid.
Similarities between an unnamed Kambara and other Australian crocodilians were noted after the Murgon mandible was described in 1982.
The species K. implexidens was not recognized as distinct until nearly complete skulls were discovered in 1993.

The flattened skull shape and depositional environment suggest Kambara were semi-aquatic ambush predators like modern crocodilians, and researchers believe it was a semi-aquatic generalist with a flat snout similar to modern crocodiles. Its skeleton shows no specializations for aquatic life beyond modern crocodilians, suggesting a generalized semi-aquatic lifestyle.

A hypothesis suggests Kambara's overbite functioned like mammalian carnassial teeth to break and slice prey, while researcher Buchanan suggested that the fused tooth sockets in Kambara molnari focused bite force to enhance puncturing ability.

The shortening of Kambara's humeral shaft might have allowed for faster lower limb movement, but this is unclear because the lower forelimb has not been described. Kambara possessed some traits for moving on land, but these were not as developed as expected for a fully terrestrial animal. Researchers suggest Kambara might have had a fibular condyle allowing hinge-like knee movement, but this cannot be confirmed because the fossil element is poorly preserved.

Fossils of adults, eggshells, and hatchlings found at Murgon suggest Kambara may have nested at this site, likely close to the water's edge, possibly within a 100-meter radius. Researchers hypothesize that Kambara nested during the dry season to time hatching with the wet season.

Phylogenetic analyses generally recover Kambara as one of the earliest diverging mekosuchines, and it was recognized as the earliest branching member of the Mekosuchinae group. The genus Kambara was described by Willis et al. in 1993.
Willis and colleagues included Mekosuchus in the group and redefined Mekosuchidae as Mekosuchinae.
Remains of Kambara are exclusively known from the Paleogene of Australia, and it was an extinct Mekosuchinae crocodilian that lived during the Eocene and Oligocene in modern-day Australia.
The Rundle Formation, inhabited by K. molnari and K. taraina, is thought to represent lagoonal mud flats.
It is debated how the coexisting species K. murgonensis and K. implexidens differed in their ecological niches despite anatomical differences.
It is debated whether Rundle Formation fossils belong to another Kambara species or a different genus, as they display "pelvic form two" with deeper peduncles shared with younger mekosuchines.
